text_blocks.snippet: The double-helix structure of DNA was discovered in 1953 by James Watson and Francis Crick, who built upon the critical X-ray diffraction data and images produced by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.

James Watson and Francis Crick: The University of Cambridge scientists who formulated the physical double-helix model of DNA and published their findings in April 1953. They shared the 1962 Nobel Prize with Maurice Wilkins.

Rosalind Franklin: The chemist and X-ray crystallographer at King's College London whose meticulous work—including the famous "Photo 51"—provided the essential experimental evidence of the helical structure. Her crucial data were shown to Watson without her permission, significantly aiding his and Crick's breakthrough.
Maurice Wilkins: Franklin's colleague at King's College London who shared her X-ray images with Watson and Crick and contributed complementary experimental data.
